content: Podiatry, also known as podiatric medicine or chiropody, is a specialized field of healthcare that focuses on the study, diagnosis, and treatment of disorders affecting the foot, ankle, knee, leg, and hip, collectively referred to as the lower extremity. The scope of practice for podiatry varies depending on the regulations established by national, state, or provincial jurisdictions. Practitioners in this field include podiatrists, chiropodists, and podiatric surgeons. The professional care of feet has ancient origins, with evidence from ancient Egypt showing depictions of foot and hand care in bas-relief carvings at the entrance to Ankmahor's tomb, dating back to 2400 BC. Hippocrates described corns and calluses, emphasizing the importance of reducing hard skin and addressing the underlying causes. He invented skin scrapers, which were precursors to modern scalpels. The Roman scientist Aulus Cornelius Celsus is credited with naming corns, while Paul of Aegina in the 7th century AD provided detailed descriptions of corns and their treatment through paring and pumice use. Until the early 20th century, chiropodists, now known as podiatrists, operated independently of organized medicine. They were licensed physicians specializing in the treatment of the feet, ankles, and related leg structures. Lewis Durlacher was among the first to advocate for a regulated profession, attempting to establish an association of practitioners in 1854. By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, professional societies and schools for chiropody were established in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia, marking the formalization of the field. The first American journal on chiropody appeared in 1907, followed by a UK journal in 1912. The profession expanded significantly after World War I and World War II, driven by the need to employ ex-soldiers and address their foot-related issues. A podiatrist, also referred to as a foot doctor, is a healthcare professional dedicated to the study and medical treatment of disorders of the foot, ankle, and lower extremity. In countries like the United Kingdom, Germany, New Zealand, and parts of Canada, the term chiropodist is often used interchangeably with podiatrist, though podiatrist is becoming the preferred term. In the UK, the titles podiatrist and chiropodist are protected and can only be used by individuals registered with the Health Professions Council (HPC). Registration typically requires a specialized bachelor's degree or diploma in podiatry from one of the recognized schools in the UK. Podiatrists in the UK primarily focus on non-invasive treatments but can perform minor surgical procedures, such as nail surgery, under local anesthesia. In Australia, podiatry is classified as an allied health profession, regulated by state boards of podiatry. Australian podiatrists complete a 3to 4-year undergraduate degree, with the first two years covering biomedical sciences and the latter years focusing on podiatry-specific areas such as biomechanics, orthopedics, pharmacology, and surgical techniques. Podiatric surgeons in Australia undergo additional training in medicine, pharmacology, and foot surgery, culminating in a master's degree and fellowship status after extensive clinical and surgical training. The prescribing rights of Australian podiatrists vary by state. While all podiatrists can use local anesthesia for minor surgical procedures, some states allow suitably qualified podiatrists to prescribe certain medications. For example, Victorian graduates may soon be authorized to prescribe Schedule 4 poisons, while podiatrists in Western Australia and South Australia with advanced training in pharmacology can already do so. In New Zealand, podiatry became a registered profession in 1969, requiring a three-year training program. The profession evolved from chiropody to podiatry, with the establishment of the New Zealand School of Podiatry in 1970. By 1976, podiatrists gained the legal right to use local anesthesia and perform minor surgical procedures. In 1984, they were granted the right to refer patients directly for X-rays, and by 1989, suitably trained podiatrists could take X-rays themselves. Diagnostic radiographic training is now incorporated into the degree syllabus. In the United States, podiatry encompasses a broader spectrum of medical practice, including both medical and surgical procedures for the foot, ankle, and lower extremity. Podiatrists complete a four-year podiatric medical school program, followed by a twoor three-year residency. Their training includes rotations in emergency medicine, internal medicine, orthopedics, and general surgery, with a focus on foot and ankle care. Podiatrists can independently diagnose, treat, prescribe medications, and perform surgeries. Board certification is available through specialty boards such as the American Board of Podiatric Orthopedics and Primary Podiatric Medicine and the American Board of Podiatric Surgery. The practice of podiatry has evolved significantly, with practitioners now working in various settings, including private practices, hospitals, and multidisciplinary clinics. Some podiatrists specialize in sports medicine, treating athletes with foot and ankle injuries, while others focus on diabetic foot care or geriatric patients. Surgical podiatrists often perform complex reconstructive procedures and minimally invasive surgeries. The demand for podiatrists is expected to grow, albeit slowly, due to the long careers of practitioners. In the United States, there are currently eight colleges of podiatric medicine, governed by the American Association of Colleges of Podiatric Medicine (AACPM), which aims to enhance academic podiatric medicine. Podiatry continues to develop as a medical specialty, addressing a wide range of foot and lower extremity conditions through both conservative and surgical approaches.
